stories.head: Nearly 40 evacuated, valley roads shut. When Paradise Valley could reopen
stories.dek: Close to 40 Squamish Nation members have been evacuated in the Squamish Valley and Paradise Valley is told to shelter in place, after the Elaho ran past its highest published peak and the Squamish hit its biggest since 2003. Reopening Paradise Valley Road hangs on one river gauge.
stories.take: As of 3 p.m. Thursday: Paradise Valley Road is closed at the Paradise Valley Bailey Bridge and Squamish Valley Road at the Pilchuck Bailey Bridge. The District expects flooding on the Paradise Valley road to end once the river at the Brackendale gauge drops below 450 cubic metres per second. We read that as the Cheakamus gauge, which was at 514 at 2:35 p.m. Squamish Nation flood line: 604-982-9938, 24 hours a day.
stories.body:
## The short version

[[glance]]

- **The people:** close to 40 Squamish Nation members in the Squamish Valley have been evacuated, the Nation said Thursday. Its team went door to door, including to anyone who could be cut off if Fergie's Bridge, a different Squamish Valley Road crossing from the closed Pilchuck bridge, has to close. The Squamish Chief reports evacuees are being given a place to stay and care. The Nation asks for care around **Lewis Drive and Moody Lane**, where the water was still rising.
- **Paradise Valley:** the District of Squamish has a shelter in place advisory for the mapped area of Paradise Valley, including the Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch area. If you can safely stay where you are, stay. If your spot starts to flood, go to higher ground. The map is linked from the [regional district's flood notice](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/inside-slrd/news-notices/November2026Flood). Questions: District emergency centre, 778-655-3020.
- **The rivers peaked overnight and Thursday morning** and are falling slowly.
- **Rain returns Friday, with more on Sunday,** but colder, and the province's river forecast stays far below this week's peak. Details below.

## When Paradise Valley could reopen

The District gave one number to watch for Paradise Valley. "Once the river level at the Water Survey of Canada Brackendale gauge is below 450 cubic metres per second, road flooding should cease," said Alex Preston, the District's public information officer.

**Which gauge?** There are two Water Survey gauges near Brackendale, one on the Squamish and one on the Cheakamus. The District did not say which. We read it as the Cheakamus gauge, for two reasons: the Cheakamus is the river that runs past Paradise Valley, and BC Hydro's own flow notices call that gauge (08GA043) "WSC's Brackendale Gauge". The Squamish gauge is running in the thousands this week, so 450 only makes sense for the Cheakamus.

**Where it stands:**

- **Peak:** 656 at 7:55 a.m. Thursday
- **11:35 a.m.:** 580
- **2:35 p.m.:** 514, roughly 60 to 75 above the line

**Our rough estimate: this evening at the earliest, somewhere around 6 to 10 p.m. Thursday.** In the early afternoon it fell about 20 an hour, which would cross 450 around 6 p.m. Through the late morning it fell only about 12 an hour, which would take until about 10 p.m. The readings jump up and down by about 20 every few minutes, rivers rarely fall in a straight line, and BC Hydro controls part of this river through the Cheakamus Dam, so treat that as a rough guide. No one has announced a reopening time, and the District said flooding should end, not that the road will open at once. [Watch the gauge live](https://wateroffice.ec.gc.ca/report/real_time_e.html?stn=08GA043), and check [DriveBC](https://www.drivebc.ca/) before you go.

**Squamish Valley Road is a different river.** It floods from the Squamish River, not the Cheakamus, so the 450 number does not apply, and no one has said when it could reopen. DriveBC lists it as closed by flooding from the 3 km mark to north of the Pilchuck Creek bridge. The province's forecast has the Squamish falling under 1,000 by Friday morning. On Paradise Valley Road, the Bailey bridge is the only road access to the homes, businesses and services on the north side, [the regional district says](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/node/6701).

**The dam.** BC Hydro's release from the Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake peaked about 5 a.m. Thursday, the District said. BC Hydro is cutting it slowly through the day, with two goals: make room in the reservoir for the next storm, and get the river back under its banks so the road can reopen.

## What the weekend brings

The rainfall warning ended Thursday morning, and the District and the Nation said heavy rain is no longer expected through Friday. The BC River Forecast Centre's outlook, issued 8 a.m. Thursday, expects another round of storms over the South Coast Friday and Saturday, with "substantial flood hazard" from the South Coast through Howe Sound and east to Pemberton.

What the newest numbers show for Squamish:

- **Rain:** the Open-Meteo weather model puts about 31 mm over the watershed on Friday, mostly in the daytime, about 19 mm Saturday, 46 mm Sunday and 19 mm Monday. For scale, the Squamish Airport had 122 mm on Wednesday alone.
- **Colder:** the freezing level is about 2,000 metres Friday and about 1,300 to 1,600 by the weekend, far below Wednesday's 2,860, so more of it should fall as snow up high instead of running straight into the rivers.
- **The river:** the province's newest Squamish River forecast, issued 11:19 a.m. Thursday, has its middle forecast falling under 1,000 by Friday morning and to about 200 by Saturday, then rising again with Sunday's rain to about 440, possibly up to 600. This week's peak was 2,370.

Forecasts can change, and this rain lands on soaked ground. Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky remain under the province's Flood Warning, the regional district says.

**What to do:**

- **Do not walk or drive through floodwater,** and stay away from fast water and riverbanks, the Nation says.
- **Sandbags:** self serve at the north end of Brennan Park Recreation Centre.
- **Our suggestions, from the province's [PreparedBC flood guide](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/emergency-management/preparedbc/know-your-hazards/floods):** if you live in the Upper Squamish Valley or Paradise Valley, keep vehicles and animals off low ground and have a few days of food, water and medicine in case the road closes again.
- **Sign up for alerts** (links at the bottom).

## How high the rivers ran

These are Water Survey of Canada real time gauges. The numbers are provisional and can be revised, sometimes a lot, at extreme highs.

[[rivers]]

- **Elaho River, near its mouth:** about 1,980 at 3:20 a.m. Thursday. The highest yearly peak in its published record, which goes back to 1981 with some years missing, is 1,450, from January 2024. The water level, 8.31 metres, was also above every published yearly peak level (2012 to 2024, with 2015 missing). Treat the exact flow with care: at a flow this far past anything measured, it is estimated from the water level and is likely to be revised. It was very likely a record. By how much is less certain.
- **Cheakamus River, near Brackendale,** the river beside Paradise Valley: 656 at 7:55 a.m., its highest since 1989, when it peaked at 680. No peak was published for 1991, 1992 or 2003, and 1991 and 2003 were two of the three biggest Squamish River floods on record. It is half again the 2021 peak of 438, which put Paradise Valley on evacuation alert, and about 25 times a typical November flow of 25.8.
- **Squamish River, near Brackendale:** 2,370 at 10:55 a.m. That is past the province's 1 in 10 year flood size (2,129), which means about a 1 in 10 chance of a flood that big in any year, and short of 1 in 20 (2,441). It would be the fourth biggest published yearly peak since 1958 (seven years have none), and the biggest since 2003.

[[fold Every big Squamish River flood on record, and the Cheakamus history | 2003 tops the Squamish list at 3,140. Thursday's 2,370 would be fourth.]]

**Squamish River,** yearly peaks at the gauge near Brackendale, in cubic metres per second (Water Survey of Canada, since 1958, seven years missing):

- **1. October 18, 2003:** 3,140
- **2. October 8, 1984:** 2,610
- **3. August 30, 1991:** 2,460
- **4. November 12, 2026 (provisional):** 2,370
- **5. November 1, 1981:** 2,270
- **6. December 27, 1980:** 2,180
- **7. September 20, 2015:** 2,080
- **8. November 12, 1990:** 2,060
- **9. January 30, 2024:** 2,010
- **10. November 5, 1975:** 1,950

**Cheakamus River,** published yearly peaks higher than this week's 656: 861 (1963), 850 (1961, estimated), 841 (1984), 827 (1980), 739 (1981) and 680 (1989).

[[/fold]]

## How the night unfolded

All times Pacific, Thursday, November 12, unless noted.

- **Wednesday, 7 to 8 p.m.:** the Elaho jumps from about 1,100 to 1,310 in an hour and keeps climbing.
- **3:20 a.m.:** the Elaho peaks near 1,980.
- **About 5 a.m.:** the release from the Cheakamus Dam peaks, the District said.
- **7:55 a.m.:** the Cheakamus near Brackendale peaks at 656.
- **Morning:** the rainfall warning ends.
- **10:55 a.m.:** the Squamish River peaks near 2,370, almost exactly what the province forecast on Tuesday (about 2,360 near 9 a.m. Thursday).
- **By Thursday afternoon:** the District has opened its Emergency Operations Centre, the Squamish Nation has opened one too, close to 40 Nation members have been evacuated and Paradise Valley is under the shelter in place advisory.

## Why the Cheakamus ran so much higher than Monday's forecast

On Monday, three days ahead, the province's river model had the Cheakamus near Brackendale peaking around 393 on Thursday afternoon. It reached 656, about two thirds more, and hours earlier. The Squamish forecast, by contrast, was almost exact.

Two things feed that gauge: water BC Hydro lets out of Daisy Lake at the Cheakamus Dam, and rain on the creeks that join below the dam. BC Hydro had not published Thursday's release when we checked, so we cannot yet say how much of the gap came from each.

[[fold How much rain fell | 122 mm at the Squamish Airport on Wednesday alone, 265 mm in a week]]

- **Squamish Airport, day by day** ([Environment Canada](https://climate.weather.gc.ca/)): 72 mm from Thursday to Saturday last week, then 34 mm Sunday, 9 mm Monday, 28 mm Tuesday and **122 mm Wednesday**. That is 265 mm in seven days.
- **The 48 hours to Thursday morning:** 134 mm in Squamish, 140 mm at Porteau Cove and 138 mm in Whistler, Environment Canada said. Meteorologist Jason Ross put the storm's total at the Squamish Airport at 160 mm, the Chief reported. Port Mellon, across Howe Sound, had 306 mm since Tuesday.
- **It was warm.** Wednesday reached 13.9°C at the airport. Over the headwaters the Open-Meteo model put the freezing level near 2,860 metres early Wednesday, so most of the watershed got rain rather than snow.

[[/fold]]

## Around the corridor

- **Pemberton:** the whole village is under an evacuation alert, with an evacuation order for properties on Airport Road. Highway 99 east of Pemberton was closed both ways, the Canadian Press reported.
- **In town:** pumps at Harris Slough are moving water away from neighbouring properties, the Chief reported. On Wednesday the District asked residents to save water because high flows were affecting the wastewater treatment plant.

## Last time Paradise Valley flooded

- **November 2021:** the regional district put 35 properties in Upper Paradise Valley, along Paradise Valley Road and Mistys Lane, on evacuation alert, and BC Hydro issued a spill notice for the Cheakamus Dam ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2021/11/15/evacuation-alert-issued-for-upper-paradise-valley/)). The Cheakamus peaked at 438 that year.
- **January 2024:** floodwater covered Squamish Valley Road ([CTV News](https://www.ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/floodwaters-inundate-squamish-valley-road/)), with the Squamish River at about 2,010.
- **October 2003, the record:** about 100 people were ordered out of their homes and about 200 more left the next day ([CBC News](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/b-c-flood-evacuations-continue-1.362893)).

More on how Squamish manages flood risk is on our [flood protection page](/issues/flood-protection/).

## Getting help

- **Emergency or a downed power line:** 911
- **Squamish Nation Public Safety Line, flooding:** 604-982-9938, 24 hours a day, or public_safety@squamish.net. It can also connect members to outreach and the crisis response team.
- **Squamish Nation Wellness team:** 604-982-7816 or wellness@squamish.net. Healthy Hubs at 1221 Chief Billy Drive and 41139-B Government Road.
- **District of Squamish emergency centre, about the Paradise Valley advisory:** 778-655-3020
- **District public works, flooding in town:** 604-815-6868, after hours 604-815-4040
- **Squamish Lillooet Regional District:** 1-800-298-7753. Medical, mobility or transport needs: call its emergency centre early at 604-384-7357.
- **If you had to leave home:** register for Emergency Support Services at [ess.gov.bc.ca](https://ess.gov.bc.ca), or call the Canadian Red Cross at 1-888-800-6493. Squamish Nation members can also call the Public Safety Line.
- **Alerts:** the Nation's [Voyent Alert!](https://www.squamish.net/stay-connected/voyent-alert/), the District's [Squamish Alert](https://squamish.ca/alert) and the regional district's [SLRD Alert](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/SLRDAlert)
- **Roads:** [DriveBC](https://www.drivebc.ca/), 1-800-550-4997. **River levels:** our [Today page](/today/).

The Nation says it will keep updating [its post](https://www.squamish.net/emergency-operations-centre-activated-due-to-flooding-2/). We will update this story as things change.

[[note]]

River flows are in cubic metres of water passing the gauge each second, from Water Survey of Canada real time data read about 3 p.m. Thursday. Real time numbers are provisional and are often revised, especially at extreme highs, where flow is estimated from the water level. Records compare with the Water Survey's published yearly peaks, which have gaps. Flood sizes (1 in 10 year and so on) are the BC River Forecast Centre's for the Squamish River near Brackendale. Monday's Cheakamus forecast and Tuesday's Squamish forecast are from the province's river model, as we reported on November 9. Daily airport rain is from Environment Canada. The 48 hour totals are Environment Canada's, as reported by the Canadian Press and the Squamish Chief. Rain and freezing level forecasts are from the Open-Meteo model. The "6 to 10 p.m." estimate is our own arithmetic from the Cheakamus gauge, not an official time.

[[/note]]

stories.head: Paradise Valley residents told to shelter in place under flood alert
stories.dek: Stay where you are and watch for official updates, The Squamish Chief reported Thursday.
stories.take: We will update this story as official information comes in.
stories.body:
## What we know

If you are in immediate danger, call 911.

[The Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-activates-emergency-operations-centre-13010625) on Thursday, November 12, 2026, that residents in Paradise Valley have been told to shelter in place under a flood alert.

Shelter in place means staying indoors where you are rather than leaving.

## What we don't know yet

The information available to us so far does not say:

- who issued the alert
- what is causing the flooding
- how many homes it covers
- how long it is expected to last

We will not guess. The Squamish Chief report linked above may have more details, and we will update this story if we learn more.

## Where to check

- Read the full report from [The Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-activates-emergency-operations-centre-13010625)
- Follow official emergency alerts for your area.
- See river levels, weather and Highway 99 conditions on our [today page](/today/)
- Background on local flood risk is on our [flood protection page](/issues/flood-protection/)

**Update, Thursday afternoon:** the District's advisory covers the mapped area of Paradise Valley, including the Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch area. Questions: the District emergency centre at 778-655-3020. River levels and when the road could reopen are in our [latest flood story](/news/squamish-valley-flood-evacuations-roads-closed/).

$0.71 million is in staff's base (two firefighters, pedestrian bridge staff and more), plus about $0.49 million council kept in September (a labour relations advisor, a fleet mechanic and more).
Pause the step up in repair savings (asset reserve)

This is the yearly increase, not all repair savings. It's a policy council chose in 2023, and the main capital reserve already starts 2027 at $3.9 million against a $13.1 million target. On October 6 council asked staff for options to raise it, not lower it (unofficial Council Watch summary).
Staff haven't priced any. After the 2024 union agreement, council cut about $600,000 (according to an unofficial Council Watch summary).
Shift more of the tax to business and industry

Doesn't lower the total, it moves who pays: homes less, businesses and industry more. Raising the major industry rate mostly lands on Woodfibre, and District policy sets that money aside, so it wouldn't help the daily budget unless the policy changes.
Use Woodfibre LNG's tax for daily costs

District policy keeps it out of daily spending so the town doesn't depend on one company. It already pays for one time projects in the 10 year plan, Woodfibre is challenging its 2025 and 2026 taxes, and its 2027 assessment isn't known until spring.
Moves the cost from your tax bill to other bills, like water, sewer or program fees.
Signed contracts, loans and reserves already promised. Very hard to change in one year.

stories.body:
## The short version

- District staff's draft 2027 budget needs **10.4% more property tax** in total than 2026. That's about **$342 more** for an average home, before new services council already said yes to.
- **Mayor Sean Easton**, **Councillor Janice DesJardins** and **Councillor Laura Prosko** each promised a 2027 tax freeze. A decision needs four votes when all seven are there, so they need one more.
- Freezing the District's total tax means cutting, delaying or finding **at least $5.7 million**, or about $6.5 million counting what council kept in September. Staff haven't published a list of cuts, and none of the three has put a dollar figure on how.
- **Renters can feel this too.** B.C. caps yearly rent increases for current tenants, so a tax rise can't push their rent past the cap. Rent for new tenants and business rents isn't capped, and landlords factor taxes in.
- No date is set for the new council's first budget meeting or the public information night. Last year's budget passed in January.

[[glance]]

## What it means for your bill

[[calc]]

The percentages here are increases in the total tax the District collects. That total includes tax from new buildings, which is one reason the average home's bill rose 10.8% in 2026 while the total rose 12.8%. Your own bill also moves with how your home's value changed compared with others in town.

## Where the extra $5.7 million goes

About two thirds of the increase is already committed: union and staff contracts, the police contract, transit, the Cheekye debris barrier reserve and loan payments, mostly for the new Public Works Facility. The biggest choice left is how much more to save for future repairs.

[[table drivers]]

The "critical" items include two new firefighters ($345,957) and $125,000 to staff the new pedestrian bridge, which Transport Canada rules require to be staffed for at least a year (staff expect about 18 months). Staff also kept $7.24 million, the tax paid by Woodfibre LNG (liquefied natural gas), out of the daily budget entirely. More on that below.

[[poll target]]

## Who promised a freeze

Three of the seven people now on council promised zero. One more wants a full review to find savings. The other three made no freeze promise.

[[table council]]

Easton's campaign page says the freeze is meant "to create constraints and accountability for government." Prosko wrote that she'd hold taxes flat without cutting projects or services. Each has named an approach, like cutting waste, zero based budgeting, fewer middle managers or more grants. As of November 12 we found no new statement from the mayor or council on how a freeze would work.

## What a freeze would take

First, "freeze" can mean three things: no increase in the total tax the District collects, no increase for existing owners once tax from new buildings is counted, or a flat bill for the average home. The promises don't say which.

Holding the total at the 2026 level means about $5.66 million less spending, or the same amount from somewhere other than property tax, and about $6.5 million counting what council kept in September. A freeze for existing owners could need less. In 2024, staff counted tax from new buildings first, which turned a 12% total into 8.9% for existing owners. The 2027 draft doesn't show that step yet, and staff haven't published the 2027 figure.

Staff's report lists no service cuts to choose from: the space for alternatives is a blank placeholder.

[[table levers]]

[[poll lever]]

## The Woodfibre LNG money

In 2026 Woodfibre LNG paid the District about $7.24 million in property tax (the District's frequently asked questions page says $7.7 million). District policy keeps that money out of daily spending and uses it for one time projects, so the town doesn't come to depend on a single company. The 10.4% is worked out without it.

On September 22 the previous council turned down a 10 year tax deal with Woodfibre, 5 to 2. Andersen voted for the deal. Regular taxation continues, and the District is defending Woodfibre's legal challenges to its 2025 and 2026 taxes. Easton, Prosko, DesJardins and Veltkamp said during the campaign they want a better deal. Ellis said Woodfibre should help pay for the capital plan through regular taxes or a fair deal. Andersen voted for the old deal, and Perreault said he would have supported it. The plant's 2027 assessment, and so its 2027 tax, won't be known until spring. Separate Woodfibre and FortisBC payments of $1.35 million each fund a District major projects team in 2027 and are expected to end after that.

[[poll wlng]]

## Behind on repairs

Staff wrote in their October 6 report: "following decades of insufficient investment in capital infrastructure and reserve building, available reserves remain constrained." The District's main capital reserve starts 2027 at $3.9 million, against a minimum target of about $13.1 million. Under the current plan it drops to about $2 million in 2028 and doesn't reach the target until 2034.

Big bills are coming. The landfill fills up in late 2029 or early 2030, and construction on a $27.8 million expansion has to start by the end of 2027. The 10 year capital plan is $357 million, and another $58.7 million of priority projects have no funding source yet. Debt payments rise to 14% of revenue, under the District's own 20% limit.

[[poll repairs]]

## The community safety package

On September 29 the previous council voted unanimously to send a $580,000 package back for public input: two bylaw officers ($259,450), a Community Safety Plan ($200,000) and BC Housing support work for people without homes ($121,000). It would add about 1.1%, or $35 on an average home. The new council decides whether it comes back.

[[poll safety]]

[[fold Main new items council looked at | What was kept, removed or sent back on September 29]]

[[table pending]]

[[/fold]]

## The bigger picture

[[bars history]]

Squamish has raised its total property tax by about 12% or more for three years running. Staff point to a fast growing town that put off saving for repairs for years, new firefighters and police, loans for the Public Works Facility, and more loans coming for the dikes and the Mamquam Bridge deck.

[[table towns]]

During the campaign Easton called 12.8% "the highest in the province." Langford's 2026 draft was higher, but Squamish was well above every nearby town we checked.

**And 2028 looks bigger.** Staff forecast **12.7% for 2028**. New police positions that a reserve has partly covered until now land fully on the tax bill (2.3%). Loans for the Mamquam Bridge deck, the Xwu'nekw Park sea dike and raising the Squamish River dikes add 2.8%, and transit expansion adds 1.5%. A 2027 freeze paid for with one time money or a pause in repair savings would carry into 2028, on top of that forecast. After 2028 the forecast eases: 7.9% in 2029, 5.7% to 7.1% through 2032, and about 4% a year from 2033. Prosko's promise covers both 2027 and 2028.

## What happens next

- **Council budget workshop for the new council:** date not set. A November 10 meeting was cancelled.
- **Public information night:** staff said it was planned for November. No date is posted yet.
- **Adoption:** an unofficial summary of staff's early timeline pointed to December. Last year's plan passed January 13. The new council sets the pace.
- **Tax rates and bills:** rates are set in spring 2027, after BC Assessment's revised roll, and bills follow.
- **Hear when dates are set:** [get the free Friday email](#signup).
- **Next regular council meeting:** [Tuesday, November 17 at 6 p.m.](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/) Its agenda isn't out yet.

## How to have your say

- Answer the questions on this page, and say what you'd keep or cut in the comments below.
- Email the District at budgetfeedback@squamish.ca. It goes to council and into a What We Heard report.
- Read the reports and answer the District's questions at [Let's Talk Squamish: Budget 2027](https://letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027).
- [Write to council or speak at a meeting](/have-your-say/).

We'll update this story when the new council's budget dates are set. Background: [Will Squamish property taxes go up in 2027?](/explained/will-squamish-property-taxes-go-up-in-2027/) and [Why taxes went up 12.8% in 2026](/explained/why-squamish-property-taxes-went-up-12-8-percent/).

[[note]]

Most numbers come from the District's staff reports of [September 29](https://letstalksquamish.ca/download_file/805/684) and [October 6, 2026](https://squamish.civicweb.net/FileStorage/29FAAEA5B2BA4D758A8067109A22B35E-2027-2036%20Financial%20Plan%20-%20Capital%20Projects%20-%20Repo.pdf). The $342 is staff's figure for an average home. The $5.66 million, the $546,000 per 1%, the $6.5 million and the 11.9% and 13% estimates are our own arithmetic from those tables. What council kept or sent back comes from an [unofficial Council Watch summary](https://squamish.councilwatchnews.com/archive/council-watch-special-business-meeting-29-sep-2026/) until minutes are posted. Other towns: [Whistler](https://www.whistler.ca/news/budget-2026-what-you-need-to-know/), [West Vancouver](https://westvancouver.ca/government-administration/financial-information/budget), [North Vancouver District](https://docs.dnv.org/documents/tax-newsletter-2026.pdf), [Langford](https://langford.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Reduction-Options-for-the-2026-Tax-Increase.pdf), [Port Moody](https://www.portmoody.ca/news-and-notices/posts/council-approves-provisional-budget-with-reductions-to-lower-tax-rate-increase-for-port-moody-residents/), [Kamloops](https://cfjctoday.com/2026/04/15/kamloops-council-finalizes-financial-plan-tax-increase-amid-opposition-from-mayor/), [Vancouver](https://www.ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/vancouver-council-votes-for-0-per-cent-property-tax-increase-in-2026/). Woodfibre vote: [Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/09/23/squamish-council-rejects-woodfibre-lng-tax-deal/).

[[/note]]

stories.body:
## The short version

- A strategic plan is council's to do list for its four year term. It doesn't need a bylaw, but it drives what goes in every budget.
- The District says the new council's strategic planning happens **January to March 2027**. No dates are posted yet.
- Last time it was adopted **192 days after election day** (175 days after council was sworn in). It was drafted in workshops with senior staff and shown in public a week before the vote. We found **no survey or public input step** before it was adopted.
- The last plan's report card is mixed. Parks and the Squamish Nation relationship were delivered. Brennan Park, the Civic Block and new jobs land weren't. The climate target is far off track by the District's own numbers.

[[glance]]

[[poll top]]

## How the last plan did

The 2023 to 2026 plan had four themes (a connected and livable community, resilient people and relationships, reliable services, and being prepared for the future) and 16 goals. Here are ten of the biggest commitments.

[[table scorecard]]

The District's final Summary of Results, presented to the outgoing council in October, lists completed projects. It doesn't mention the emissions numbers or the Woodfibre agreement, and the only item it lists under the jobs land goal is a data tool. Community emissions include things the District doesn't control, like highway traffic and provincial building rules. Progress through the term was reported as the share of planned projects finished (about 40% complete and 40% on track by September 2025), not as numbers like homes built or bus riders.

Plans also change mid term. In April 2024 council narrowed more than 115 tasks down to 38 priorities, after a staff report said "the solution is not more resources in the form of higher budgets or more Staff". In early 2025 it scored the list again, and in May it dropped the items ranked "may do" and "may not do".

[[poll measure]]

## What the seven promised

Six of the seven were not on the last council. Only Eric Andersen was.

[[table members]]

At the swearing in on November 3, Mayor Easton named four needs he'd heard from residents: housing locals can afford; more recreation, culture and arts; social and health services for all ages; and transportation that works. He asked to be judged on one question: "Did we meaningfully and measurably improve the quality of life for residents?"

## Where they agree, and where they split

[[table agree]]

A decision needs a majority of the members at the meeting, four when all seven are there. So items with four or more names are the likeliest to make the new plan.

Where they differ:

- **Parking:** Easton, DesJardins, Perreault and Prosko want to stop letting new buildings provide less parking than the rules require. Andersen would judge each case. Ellis wants the rules matched to how many cars people actually own.
- **The growth boundary and the Cheema lands:** Andersen and DesJardins are open to housing there. Ellis opposes widening the boundary without a plan to service it and land for affordable homes. Veltkamp would wait until already planned areas are built.
- **Brennan Park:** Prosko wants a second ice rink started in 2027, Ellis wants the task force sped up, and Easton wants Woodfibre to help pay for a pool and rink. Perreault wants a funding plan first. DesJardins wants a referendum on a big expansion.
- **Bike lanes and sidewalks:** Easton would pause new upgrades until residents are consulted. Ellis would add safe routes.

[[poll climate]]

## How the plan gets made

In the last round, council was sworn in November 1, 2022 and endorsed its plan on April 25, 2023. Staff describe the process as "several facilitated workshops that take into account individual Council member agendas, the OCP, current pressing community issues and ongoing District initiatives." (The OCP is the Official Community Plan, the town's long term land use bylaw.)

The public record shows closed council sessions in those months, including a four and a half hour session on March 20, 2023, held under section 90(1)(l) of the Community Charter, which covers "municipal objectives, measures and progress reports." B.C. councils commonly use that section for planning sessions, and closing them is legal. The minutes don't name the topic, so we can't confirm those were the planning workshops. The draft was then presented in public on April 18 and adopted a week later. We found no survey or public input step before adoption. A June 2023 District release, which we could only see in a search index, listed events to share it after adoption: the farmers market, a Chamber of Commerce lunch and a drop in with the mayor.

B.C. law requires a public consultation on the five year financial plan, which council adopts each year, but not on a strategic plan, so whether residents get a say first is up to council. The District did run a random sample Citizen Satisfaction Survey in spring 2025, which it said would help inform strategic planning and budgets.

[[poll input]]

## Why it matters for your tax bill

Staff write that "the Strategic Plan informs the Financial Plan." The draft 2027 budget, with its 10.4% base increase, says it is "aligned with the District's 2023-2026 Strategic Plan", the old council's plan. So the new council will likely vote on its first budget before it has written its own priorities. That's normal: the last council's first budget came in December 2022, months before its plan, and a budget can be amended later in the year. Read more: [Staff say $342 more. The mayor promised $0. Here's what decides your bill](/news/squamish-2027-budget-tax-freeze-explained/).

The draft budget also carries $75,000 to recruit a new chief administrative officer, the District's top staff job and the one staff member who reports directly to council, because the current one, Linda Glenday, plans to retire ([staff report, September 29](https://letstalksquamish.ca/download_file/805/684)). Perreault and Veltkamp both campaigned on hiring a new one.

## What happens next

- **Strategic planning:** January to March 2027, according to the District's briefing for candidates. No workshop dates are posted.
- **Budget:** the new council's first budget workshop and a public information night are still to be scheduled.
- **Next regular council meeting:** [Tuesday, November 17 at 6 p.m.](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/)
- **Council meetings in 2027:** the first and third Tuesday of most months, starting January 5.

## Have your say

- Answer the questions on this page and add your comment below. It's all public, so council can read it too.
- Tell council directly: email council@squamish.ca, or [write to council or speak at a meeting](/have-your-say/).
- Add specific asks to [What Squamish Wants](/wants/), where residents vote yes or no on things like pickleball courts and crosswalks.

We'll follow the plan as it's written and track each goal once it's adopted.

stories.head: Recent overdoses hit Squamish Nation. Where to get help and free naloxone
stories.dek: Squamish Nation, under a State of Emergency since December 2024, shares where to get free naloxone, counselling and weekly drug checking, including a Monday mobile service in the Squamish Valley.
stories.take: Anyone affected by the toxic drug crisis, including grief or loss, can call Squamish Nation's Háhalhi7iwan (Wellness) Department at 604-982-7816; in an overdose, call 911.
stories.body:
## If you need help now

- In an overdose: call 911 right away, give naloxone if you have it and follow the emergency instructions. Do not leave the person alone.
- Support from Squamish Nation's Háhalhi7iwan (Wellness) Department: 604-982-7816

## What is happening

Squamish Nation (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw) says its community continues to feel the impact of the toxic drug crisis, including several recent overdoses. The Nation is still operating under the State of Emergency its Council declared in December 2024 to support public safety measures.

The Nation says recent losses are a reminder of how serious the crisis is. It says the unregulated drug supply has become more unpredictable, often with unexpected and very dangerous contaminants, so anyone using unregulated substances may be at risk of drug poisoning.

## Where to get support

The Háhalhi7iwan (Wellness) Department offers therapy and counselling and weekly programs, including Wellness Wednesdays on the North Shore and in the Squamish Valley. It can also help people get into treatment and detox. It welcomes anyone affected, including people going through grief or loss.

- Phone: 604-982-7816
- Email: Wellness@squamish.net

## How to lower the risk

- Carry naloxone, which can reverse an opioid overdose. It is free from the vending machine or front desk at 380 Welch Street, Unit 4.
- Avoid using alone. If possible, have someone nearby who can respond in an emergency. If you are alone, call the National Overdose Response Service at 1-888-688-6677 or use the LifeGuard App.
- Know the signs of an overdose: slow or irregular breathing, not responding, gurgling, choking or unusual snoring sounds, and blue, grey or pale lips or fingertips.

## Weekly drug checking

Drug checking means testing a drug sample for dangerous contents. Only the Monday service is in the Squamish Valley. The Wednesday and Friday sessions are on the Capilano Reserve.

- Mondays, 1:30 to 3:30 p.m.: mobile drug checking in the Squamish Valley. Call 604-982-7816 to arrange.
- Wednesdays, 1:30 to 3:30 p.m.: Ikwiks and Kwumkwum, under the Lions Gate Bridge, Capilano Reserve.
- Fridays, 1:30 to 3:30 p.m.: Lower Capilano Road and Lawa Road, next to Estítkw Place, Capilano Reserve.

Read the Nation's full notice at [squamish.net](https://www.squamish.net/toxicdrugcrisisresponse/). More local safety news is on our [policing and safety page](/issues/policing-and-safety/).

stories.head: Squamish River could near a 1 in 50 year flood this week, its biggest since 2003
stories.dek: The middle forecast is a 1 in 10 to 1 in 20 year flood, the biggest since 2003, peaking about 9 a.m. Thursday. The top of the province's range is past a 1 in 50 year flood, and the river can go higher than its range. The Upper Squamish Valley has no dikes and one road out. Most of town sits behind dikes. Live numbers, charts and what to do before Tuesday night.
stories.take: The Squamish River is forecast to rise fast all day Wednesday, pass 2,000 cubic metres per second about 8 p.m. and peak near 2,360 about 9 a.m. Thursday, with a possible range of about 1,210 to 2,915. A provincial Flood Watch is in effect, which means flooding is possible, not certain.
stories.body:
## The short version

[[glance]]

[[warn]]

[[timeline]]

[[fold Read the full short version | How big, the worst and mildest cases, official status, highway, schools and Remembrance Day]]

- **Who is at risk:** the Upper Squamish Valley, the rural valley along Squamish Valley Road north of town. It has no dikes and one road in and out. Paradise Valley is also exposed.
- **Do now:** if you are on low ground in the Upper Squamish Valley or Paradise Valley, move animals, vehicles, trailers and feed in daylight on Tuesday. Aim to be done by mid afternoon, well before dark.
- **In town:** most of town sits behind dikes, which lower the risk but do not remove it. On higher ground, like Garibaldi Highlands or Valleycliffe, the river is not your risk: the drive, blocked storm drains and power cuts are. Expect pooled water on roads and closed river trails, and stay off dikes and riverbanks Wednesday to Friday.
- **How big:** the province's river model has the Squamish River peaking near **2,360 cubic metres per second** at the gauge near Brackendale, about 9 a.m. Thursday. On the province's own scale that is between a 1 in 10 and a 1 in 20 year flood, and it would be the highest flow since the October 2003 flood.
- **A way to picture it:** the middle forecast is about 17% more water than the January 2024 high water, which put water over Squamish Valley Road. The top of the forecast range is closer to the 2003 flood than to 2024.
- **How bad it could get:** the top of the range is about 2,915, past a 1 in 50 year flood (2,843) and short of a 1 in 100 year flood (3,137). The province says the real flow can land above its range.
- **How mild it could be:** the bottom of the range is about 1,210, less than the high water the river sees every second year.
- **Official status, Tuesday morning:** the province has a Flood Watch out, which means flooding is possible, not certain. We found no evacuation alerts or orders on the regional district's list. The live panel above checks both every five minutes.
- **Highway, schools and Remembrance Day:** Highway 99 was open late Monday night, but Environment Canada warns some roads may become impassable, so check [DriveBC](https://www.drivebc.ca/) before you drive Wednesday or Thursday. Wednesday is a school holiday. For Thursday, the school district posts any closure by 7 a.m. at [sd48seatosky.org](https://www.sd48seatosky.org/). The outdoor ceremony at the cenotaph is just before 11 a.m. Wednesday, in the heaviest rain, and we have not seen any change announced.

[[/fold]]

[[fold The timeline in words | Every step of the province's newest forecast, Monday night to Saturday]]

**The timeline.** This is the province's forecast for the Squamish River, issued 9:20 a.m. Tuesday:

- **Monday, 10 p.m.:** the river was at 237 and falling. It is calm before the rain.
- **Tuesday, November 10:** heavy rain starts, but the river stays low most of the day, around 200 to 300.
- **Overnight Tuesday into Wednesday:** the river starts climbing fast.
- **Wednesday morning, about 8 a.m.:** past 1,000 and still rising quickly. Wednesday is Remembrance Day.
- **Wednesday, about noon:** past 1,351, the size of high water the river sees every second year.
- **Wednesday evening, about 8 p.m.:** past 2,000. In January 2024, about 2,010 put water over Squamish Valley Road.
- **Wednesday, about 11 p.m.:** past the 1 in 10 year mark of 2,129, and still rising.
- **Thursday, November 12, about 9 a.m.:** the peak, near 2,360.
- **The high edge of the forecast band** crosses the 1 in 10 year mark by about 8 a.m. Wednesday, so a higher and earlier peak is possible.
- **Thursday, about 6 p.m.:** back just under 2,000.
- **Friday, about 9 a.m.:** about 900 and falling.
- **Saturday afternoon:** a second, smaller bump near 580 from Friday's rain.

The river is forecast to stay above 2,000 for about 22 hours, from about 8 p.m. Wednesday to about 5 p.m. Thursday. Do not read "peak Thursday morning" as having until Thursday: the river climbs fast all day Wednesday, and the high edge of the forecast gets there much sooner.

[[/fold]]

[[note]]

The live panel near the top of this page shows the newest river reading and the newest forecast, every five minutes. The numbers in the story itself are from the forecast below.

You can see the province's own chart for the Squamish River [here](https://bcrfc.env.gov.bc.ca/freshet/clever/08GA022.PDF). This story uses the run issued at 9:20 a.m. Tuesday, November 10; the first version used Monday's 10:11 a.m. run, which had a lower peak of 2,231. The province reruns it at least once a day, so check the time stamp on the chart. River numbers in this story come from that forecast unless we say otherwise. Rain and freezing level numbers come from the Open-Meteo weather model.

One caution: these numbers are flow at the gauge. Flow does not say exactly which land floods. That depends on the water level at each spot, log jams and banks giving way.

[[/note]]

## Who is most exposed

Tap your area under **What does this mean for me?** near the top of this story for your risk and what to do. In short: the Upper Squamish Valley has no dikes and one road in and out, Paradise Valley is also exposed, and most of town sits behind dikes, which lower the risk but do not remove it.

[[rivers]]

The Elaho is forecast lower than in January 2024 while the Squamish is forecast higher, which would mean more of the water comes from the other creeks and rivers along the valley this time.

## What to do

The steps for your area are under **What does this mean for me?** near the top. These apply to everyone:

- **Never drive through water on a road.** You cannot see how deep it is or whether the road is still there.
- **Stay off riverbanks, dike edges and gravel bars** from Tuesday night to Friday. Banks can give way under fast water.
- **Clear leaves from the storm drains** near your home before the heavy rain, never in moving water.
- **Follow the official sources.** The regional district's emergency page is [slrd.bc.ca/emergency-program](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/emergency-program). The District of Squamish's is [squamish.ca](https://squamish.ca/public-safety-services/emergency-program/). Evacuation alerts and orders across BC are on [EmergencyInfoBC](https://www.emergencyinfobc.gov.bc.ca/). The province's flood guide is at [PreparedBC](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/emergency-management/preparedbc/know-your-hazards/floods).

**Phone numbers, in case the internet is down:**

- **Emergency:** 911
- **Squamish Lillooet Regional District** (handles the Upper Squamish Valley and upper Paradise Valley): 1-800-298-7753. We could not find any announced place for livestock. Call before you load the trailer.
- **District of Squamish public works, for flooding in town:** 604-815-6868, after hours 604-815-4040
- **DriveBC road reports:** 1-800-550-4997
- **BC Hydro, power out or a line down:** 1-800-224-9376

[[fold Upper Squamish Valley and Paradise Valley, every step | Move animals and vehicles in daylight Tuesday. Leave Tuesday if being cut off would put you at risk.]]

- **Move animals, trailers, vehicles, feed and equipment off low ground in daylight on Tuesday.** The river is forecast to start climbing overnight Tuesday.
- **If being cut off would put you at risk, leave in daylight on Tuesday.** That means medical needs, small children or no supplies. Squamish Valley Road is the only way out and can flood before your property does. Do not count on leaving Wednesday. This is not an evacuation order. Only the regional district can issue one, and this is general preparedness advice.
- **If an evacuation order is issued, leave at once.**
- **Otherwise, be ready to be cut off.** Have three days of food, water, medicine and fuel, and charge your phones. Power and internet often go out up the valley.
- **Sign up for alerts now.** Upper Squamish Valley and upper Paradise Valley: [SLRD Alert](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/SLRDAlert). Town and lower Paradise Valley: [Squamish Alert](https://squamish.ca/alert). If you are not sure which covers you, sign up for both.
- **Know the two evacuation words.** An evacuation alert means be ready to leave. An evacuation order means leave now.

[[/fold]]

[[fold Highway, schools, power and Remembrance Day | Highway 99 open late Monday, Wednesday a school holiday, Thursday closures posted by 7 a.m.]]

- **Highway 99:** no incidents or closures between Horseshoe Bay and Whistler on [DriveBC](https://www.drivebc.ca/). Live status is on our [Today page](/today/).
- **Schools:** Wednesday is a holiday. For Thursday, the Sea to Sky School District says schools stay open unless a closure is announced, and families are told by 7 a.m. Check [sd48seatosky.org](https://www.sd48seatosky.org/).
- **Power:** heavy rain and wind bring outages. The outage map is at [bchydro.com](https://www.bchydro.com/power-outages/app/outage-map.html).
- **Remembrance Day:** details of the [ceremony](/news/squamish-remembrance-day-ceremony-2026/). Check with the [Legion](https://www.squamishlegion.ca) for any change.

[[/fold]]

## How big would this flood be?

[[ruler]]

**Where this storm would land among the 61 recorded yearly peaks:**

- **Middle forecast, 2,360:** fourth biggest of the 61 recorded yearly peaks, and the biggest since 2003. These are Water Survey of Canada's instantaneous yearly peaks, the same kind of number as the hourly forecast.
- **Top of the range, about 2,915:** second only to 2003.
- **Bottom of the range, about 1,210:** an ordinary year. The river peaked higher than that in 2021 (1,660) and last December (1,510).

Nine of the ten biggest floods came between late August and December. Only five years on record have passed the 1 in 10 year mark of 2,129: 1980, 1981, 1984, 1991 and 2003. None since. A "1 in 10 year flood" does not mean it comes every ten years. It means a one in ten chance in any single year.

[[fold Flood sizes and the ten biggest floods on record | The province's flood sizes, and the top ten years since 1958]]

River flow is measured in cubic metres of water passing the gauge each second. These are the flood sizes the BC River Forecast Centre uses for the Squamish River near Brackendale:

- **Every second year:** 1,351
- **1 in 5 year flood:** 1,809
- **1 in 10 year flood:** 2,129
- **1 in 20 year flood:** 2,441
- **1 in 50 year flood:** 2,843
- **1 in 100 year flood:** 3,137
- **October 2003, the biggest on record:** 3,140

The middle forecast of 2,360 is past the 1 in 10 year mark. The top of the range, about 2,915, is past the 1 in 50 year mark.

**The ten biggest floods on record.** The gauge has 61 published yearly peaks going back to 1958, from Water Survey of Canada. Seven years (1967, 1992, 1996, 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2020) have no published peak flow. For 2016, the recorded water level suggests a peak of about 2,000, which would put it on this list:

- **1. October 18, 2003:** 3,140
- **2. October 8, 1984:** 2,610
- **3. August 30, 1991:** 2,460
- **4. November 1, 1981:** 2,270
- **5. December 27, 1980:** 2,180
- **6. September 20, 2015:** 2,080
- **7. November 12, 1990:** 2,060
- **8. January 30, 2024:** 2,010
- **9. November 5, 1975:** 1,950
- **10. October 12, 1958:** 1,880

[[/fold]]

## What these flows did last time

Flow at the gauge is only part of the story. This is what happened on the ground at similar or bigger flows, from news reports at the time:

- **January 30, 2024, about 2,010:** the province had a Flood Warning out for the Squamish River, and CTV News reported that [floodwaters covered Squamish Valley Road](https://www.ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/floodwaters-inundate-squamish-valley-road/). This week's middle forecast is about 17% more water than that.
- **Late 2021:** on November 15, with the worst of the water on the Cheakamus, the regional district put 35 properties in Upper Paradise Valley, along Paradise Valley Road and Mistys Lane, on evacuation alert, and BC Hydro issued a spill notice for the Cheakamus Dam ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2021/11/15/evacuation-alert-issued-for-upper-paradise-valley/)). The Squamish River's own 2021 peak, about 1,660, came later, on December 2. The Cheakamus is forecast to peak near 393 this week.
- **October 2003, 3,140, the record:** Squamish ordered about 100 people out of their homes, and about 200 more left the next day. The report did not say which neighbourhoods. BC Hydro opened the flood gates at the Daisy Lake Reservoir, and a river flooded its banks and spilled into town, CBC reported ([CBC News](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/b-c-flood-evacuations-continue-1.362893)). This week's top of the range, about 2,915, is about 93% of that flow.

**What the regional district says about floods this size.** Its summary of the 2018 Upper Squamish flood study says: "At the 50-year flood event and above, most of the valley floor is flooded, with typical depths of 1 to 2 m within the inundated area." It adds that much of that water would be "dangerous for most to all people" ([regional district](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/emergency-program/hazard-reports-information/local-hazard-reports/upper-squamish-flood-hazard)). This week's middle forecast is below that 50 year size. The top of the range is just past it.

**Were you there in 2024 or 2003?** We could not find reports of exactly which stretches of road and which fields went under. If you know, [send us a tip](/tip/) and we will add it.

## The rain behind it

- **Environment Canada's warning:** 120 to 160 mm in Squamish from early Tuesday to Wednesday night, possibly more, with moderate rain into Thursday morning.
- **The mountains get more.** The Open-Meteo weather model puts about 76 mm on the Elaho headwaters Tuesday, 119 mm Wednesday and 55 mm Thursday. That is about 250 mm in three days on the ground that feeds the river.
- **The valley floor:** about 68 mm Tuesday, 57 mm Wednesday and 46 mm Thursday in the same model.
- **It follows a wet week.** The same model puts about 156 mm on the headwaters in the seven days before this storm.

## It keeps raining Friday. Why does the river peak Thursday?

A river does not peak when the rain stops. It peaks after the heaviest and warmest rain.

- **Tuesday and Wednesday are the big days.** Rain on the headwaters drops by half on Thursday and to under 20 mm on Friday.
- **Those days are also warm.** The freezing level is forecast to climb to about 2,900 metres. That is above most of the peaks, so it rains on nearly the whole watershed instead of snowing on the top half. The province's Flood Watch also warns of melt from the shallow early snowpack.
- **The river lags the rain.** The Elaho is forecast to peak Wednesday afternoon. Its water reaches Brackendale within hours and drives the Wednesday evening rise. Continued rain then holds the river up into Thursday.
- **Thursday's rain is lighter.** Once the rain eases, less water is arriving than the river is carrying away, so it falls even though it is still raining. This watershed is steep and rocky and drains in about a day.
- **Friday is colder.** The freezing level falls to roughly 1,400 metres on Friday morning, so the upper half of the watershed gets snow, and snow stays on the mountain.

One thing to watch: forecasts disagree about how much rain falls Friday. If it comes in wetter and warmer, Saturday's second bump would be bigger than forecast, on ground that is already soaked.

## The ground and the water table

Until last week it had been a dry fall. A provincial groundwater monitoring well on Paradise Valley Road hit its lowest level since readings began in 2015 at the end of October: 8.67 metres below the ground.

Then the rain came. The Open-Meteo weather model puts about 156 mm on the Squamish River headwaters in the last seven days, and the Squamish River briefly reached about 800 on Sunday. The well has risen half a metre in a week and is still well below normal for November.

What that means: this one well only tells us about Paradise Valley, and it says the ground there started this storm unusually dry underneath. It cannot tell us about the Upper Squamish Valley. As a general rule, the water table in river gravels rises with the river, so low ground and old channels beside a river can get wet before any water comes over the banks.

## Where the flood call comes from

When the District of Squamish or the regional district says there might be a flood, they are passing on a notice from the BC River Forecast Centre. The province builds it in four steps:

- **Rain forecast.** Weather models say how much rain lands on the mountains, hour by hour.
- **Freezing level and snow.** Warm storms rain on the whole watershed and melt snow. Cold storms leave snow up high.
- **River model.** The rain, the melt and the current river flow go into a model that predicts flow at each gauge for ten days.
- **Compare with past floods.** The predicted peak is compared with flood sizes, and one of three notices goes out.

The three notices, from mildest to most serious:

- **High Streamflow Advisory:** rivers rising fast, no major flooding expected.
- **Flood Watch:** rivers may reach or go over the top of their banks.
- **Flood Warning:** rivers are over their banks, or will be very soon.

Squamish is under the middle one. The province upgraded the South Coast, including Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky, to a [Flood Watch](https://bcrfc.env.gov.bc.ca/warnings/advisories/FWT_2026_11_09_1236_SC-NVI-WVI-CVI-East%20Vancouver%20Island-CC%20-%20Kingcome-Fraser%20Valley-North_UPG.pdf) at 12:36 p.m. Monday.

## What agencies and other outlets are saying

Here is how the river forecast sits beside what agencies and other news outlets have said so far:

- **Environment Canada** has an orange rainfall warning for Squamish to Whistler: 120 to 160 mm, possibly more, with flooding likely and some roads possibly impassable. See the [warning](https://weather.gc.ca/warnings/index_e.html?prov=bc).
- **The province's Flood Watch** covers the whole South Coast and Vancouver Island in general words. It says modelling shows "the potential for flows in the 5-year to 10-year range, or higher, in areas".
- **The Squamish Chief and North Shore News** have reported the rainfall warning.

The bulletin covers the whole coast, so it does not name single rivers. The forecast for each river sits one layer deeper on the province's website, as a chart for each gauge. For the Squamish River, that chart falls in the "or higher" part of the bulletin's line: the middle forecast is over the 1 in 10 year mark, and the top of the range is close to 1 in 50.

## What could change

- **The range is wide.** The forecast runs from about 1,210 to 2,915. The province says the real flow can even land outside that range.
- **It will be updated.** The province reruns the forecast at least once a day. If the storm tracks north or south, or the freezing level changes, the peak moves with it.
- **A Flood Warning would be the next step.** If the province issues one for the Squamish River, flooding is expected, not just possible.

We will update this story when the province issues a new forecast.

The Squamish River could near a 1 in 50 year flood this week. Its worst case is just under that mark, and its likely case is the biggest flood since 2003. The Upper Squamish Valley has no dikes and one road out.

The province's own numbers:

• Monday night: 237 cubic metres per second. Forecast peak: 2,231. About nine times as much water
• Climbing from overnight Tuesday, past the 1 in 10 year flood mark by Wednesday evening, near its peak into Thursday
• Top of the forecast range: 2,784, just under a 1 in 50 year flood. The bottom is an ordinary high water year
• If the middle forecast holds, the fifth biggest since records began in 1958, and bigger than the January 2024 high water that covered Squamish Valley Road
• Up to 250 mm of warm rain in the mountains in three days. Rain almost to the peaks, not snow

stories.head: Council drops closed Nov 10 meeting so its next business meeting is public
stories.dek: The new council's second business meeting was going to be a closed session for legal advice on November 10. Councillors asked to change the schedule, so their next business meeting is now the public one on Tuesday, November 17 at 6 p.m.
stories.take: The November 10 closed meeting is cancelled. The new council's next business meeting is the public one on Tuesday, November 17 at 6 p.m. in Council Chambers, and you can attend or watch live.
stories.body:
## What changed

The District of Squamish has cancelled the [special business meeting](/meetings/2026-11-10-special/) that was set for Tuesday, November 10 at 9 a.m. The District's meeting listing now reads "MEETING CANCELLED" and gives no reason.

That meeting would have been almost entirely private. Its only item was a vote to close the doors so council could get legal advice from its lawyers, which is protected by solicitor and client privilege. Residents could have watched the opening minutes and nothing more.

## Why council asked for the change

Councillor [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/) explained the change in a statement that former council candidate Anders Ourom shared in a local Facebook group:

"We didn't want our first meeting as a new Council to be a closed meeting, so we requested a change to the schedule with the CAO. We now have an orientation and meeting scheduled for Tuesday, November 10, at 9 am. We felt it was important to ensure our first meeting aligned with our commitment to transparency, and that's why we made the change."

The CAO is the chief administrative officer, the District's top staff member, who sets up council's meeting schedule.

What this means:

- The new council still meets staff on November 10, but for an orientation. It is not listed as a public meeting.
- The council's next business meeting is now **Tuesday, November 17**, and it is open to the public.
- The council was sworn in on November 3. That [inaugural meeting](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/) was a ceremony and also a business meeting: it had an agenda, and council voted on its regional district board members, the acting mayor rotation, appointments to other boards and its 2027 meeting schedule. Those votes are on the public record.

## Where and when: November 17

- **What:** [Regular council meeting](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/), the new council's first regular business meeting
- **When:** Tuesday, November 17, starting at 6 p.m.
- **Where:** Council Chambers, Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue
- **Open to the public:** yes, anyone can attend in person
- **Watch live:** [District of Squamish YouTube streams](https://www.youtube.com/@DistrictofSquamish/streams)
- **Agenda:** usually posted the Thursday before on the [District's meeting portal](https://squamish.civicweb.net/Portal/MeetingInformation.aspx?Id=2119). We will explain every item in plain language on our [meeting page](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/) once it posts.

stories.head: Got old Pokémon cards? Squamish's first card show is today, and it's free
stories.dek: If you have a shoebox of Pokémon cards at home, there is a place to trade them today. Roundhouse Martial Arts & Fitness hosts what its owners call Squamish's first Pokémon Card Show on Saturday, November 7, from noon to 3 p.m. It is free for visitors and vendors, at 38147 Cleveland Avenue.
stories.take: The free show runs today, November 7, from noon to 3 p.m. on the second floor at 38147 Cleveland Avenue.
stories.body:
## What's happening

Cole Smith and Candace Fan, who own Roundhouse Martial Arts & Fitness, are hosting a Pokémon Card Show at their gym today. They say it is the first of its kind in Squamish. Fans can buy, trade or just look at cards. Entry is free, and vendors do not pay to take part either.

The show is meant to be small. Half the space is set aside for vendors. The other half is for kids of all ages to trade cards and meet each other.

## Cards locals can afford

Some Pokémon cards sell for thousands of dollars, or even millions. Smith says he does not want cards like that at this show. He wants prices that make sense for local buyers, with cards at about:

- $5 to $20 for most cards
- maybe $50 for a few

"I don't want vendors with their $3,000 card," he said.

## Why he's doing it

Smith grew up with the cards. He was in Grade 4 when Pokémon came out. Like many kids, he stopped collecting, but his mom had kept his old cards in a bin. He got back into the hobby as an adult. The couple also collect Pokémon stuffed animals when they travel, and they now have a two month old daughter.

## What could come next

Smith says a few vendors from the city have already shown interest. If one or two small shows prove there is demand, he hopes to move to Totem Hall. He would like to hold a bigger convention there that also covers sports collections and other anime collectibles.

The Squamish Chief [reported on the show](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/on-today-squamish-pokemon-collectible-card-show-on-nov-7-12941202).

- Open to collectors, new fans and kids of all ages

stories.head: Scientists want to watch Mount Garibaldi closely. No, it isn't erupting
stories.dek: Federal scientists want to start Canada's first dedicated volcano watch on the peaks around Squamish, and the regional district has backed the idea. The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board endorsed the proposal on October 30. The five-year project would cover Mount Garibaldi, Mount Cayley and Mount Meager from April 2027, if federal funding comes through.
stories.take: Nothing changes for residents now; the regional district endorsed a federal monitoring proposal that still needs funding approval.
stories.body:
## What the project would do

The Geological Survey of Canada, part of Natural Resources Canada, wants to run a five-year project called VolCan: Towards a Canadian Volcano Observatory. It would focus on three volcanoes in the Sea to Sky: Mount Garibaldi, Mount Cayley and Mount Meager.

Under the plan, scientists would:

- Set up baseline monitoring at priority volcanoes, so they know what normal looks like
- Create notification steps and regular updates for emergency managers
- Hold workshops and emergency exercises with regional, municipal and Indigenous governments

The work would also help the federal government decide whether to create a permanent national observatory. Canada does not have one today.

## Why Squamish is in the picture

In an October 9 letter, the survey called the three peaks the most threatening volcanoes in Canada. It said debris flows and ash could reach Squamish, Whistler and Pemberton, along with Highway 99, the CN rail line, and power and communication lines.

The ratings are about possible impacts as well as activity. They do not mean an eruption is likely soon. Garibaldi and Meager are rated very high threat, and Cayley high threat.

## No sign of an eruption

Eruptions in Canada are rare. Natural Resources Canada has reported no satellite evidence of magma moving the ground at the country's volcanoes. Scientists say eruptions usually give warning signs, sometimes months or years ahead. Mount Meager had Canada's last major explosive eruption about 2,350 years ago, with ash reaching Alberta.

## What comes next

- The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board endorsed the plan on October 30 with no one opposed. Area A director Vivian Birch-Jones moved the motion.
- The survey is applying to the Canadian Safety and Security Program for money. Funding is not confirmed.
- If approved, the project would run from April 2027 to March 2032.

The plan builds on Canada's first volcanic hazard map workshop, held in Squamish on September 15 by the survey and Simon Fraser University's Centre for Natural Hazards Research.

The Squamish Chief [reported the endorsement](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/slrd-backs-proposal-for-canadas-first-volcano-observatory-12961715). For more on local hazards, see our [flood protection](/issues/flood-protection/) page.

stories.head: Why bears near Squamish rivers are easier to surprise right now
stories.dek: Bears getting ready to hibernate are busy eating and pay less attention to what is around them. The District of Squamish says they are often near berry bushes and along waterways feeding on spawning salmon. Trail users can easily spook them in a surprise encounter.
stories.take: Bears are feeding near berry bushes and salmon streams before hibernation, so trail users should expect them there and can find the District's tips on avoiding conflicts.
stories.body:
## What is happening

Bears in the Squamish area are getting ready for winter hibernation. The District of Squamish shared this in its Wildlife Wednesday post on November 6, 2026.

At this time of year, bears spend much of their time eating. The District says they are often found:

- Near berry bushes
- Along waterways, feeding on spawning salmon

## Why it matters on the trails

When bears are focused on eating, they are less aware of what is going on around them. That means they may not notice a person coming until the last moment.

The District says bears in this state can be easily spooked by trail users in surprise encounters. A surprise meeting is what can lead to a conflict between people and wildlife.

## Who it affects

This matters most for anyone using trails near berry patches, creeks and rivers where salmon are spawning. That includes people walking, running, biking or walking dogs.

## Where to find the tips

The District has tips available on preventing conflicts between people and wildlife along trails. You can find them through the District's E-News at [squamish.ca](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/enews-archives/).

stories.head: After 120 years, Brackendale's post office is gone. Where mail goes now
stories.dek: Brackendale's post office closed for good on October 31, 2026, 120 years after it opened. Canada Post could not fill the job or find a local business to host an outlet, so the service moves to Garibaldi Highlands. The neighbourhood itself is named after its first postmaster.
stories.take: Brackendale postal service has moved to Garibaldi Highlands after the Brackendale post office closed October 31, 2026.
stories.body:
## What happened

The Brackendale post office opened on August 1, 1906, and closed on October 31, 2026. [The Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/the-history-of-the-brackendale-post-office-12991206) on the closure and the history of the office.

Postal service for Brackendale has now moved to Garibaldi Highlands.

## Why it closed

This summer, Brackendale residents wrote to the District of Squamish and spoke to the newspaper about staff shortages at the office.

- Canada Post could not fill the open job.
- The job paid $45,000 a year for six days of work each week.
- The person in the job also had to cover the lease payments.

Before the closure, Canada Post wrote to the District saying it would keep service in Brackendale if a local business agreed to host a postal outlet. Mike Lee, who handles government and community affairs for Canada Post, said keeping a presence in the neighbourhood was the preferred outcome, but it depended on finding a willing retail partner. No partner was found.

## How Brackendale got its name

According to BC Geographical Names, the provincial database of place names, Brackendale is named after its first postmaster, Thomas Hirst Bracken. The database describes him as an elderly Englishman who also ran a general store and the Bracken Arms Hotel. He went back to England after the hotel burned down. The database lists the post office as closing July 18, 1912.

Squamish Library archives say Hughie Mills rebuilt the post office building in 1916 after a fire. The lot was first bought from the Judd family when they divided up their land.

## A century of mail

- 2002: the office began using a special ink stamp reading "winter home of the bald eagle."
- 2004: longtime employee Joyce Berg retired after almost 27 years. She and her husband owned the building, then seen as Brackendale's commercial centre.
- 2006: the office marked 100 years, noted by a postal history newsletter for stamp collectors.

The building once kept horse feed outside for farmers, and Government Road, where it sits, was once part of the Sea to Sky Highway.

The office faced closure before. Berg said residents started many petitions back then. "I almost got fired, but we kept our post office," she told the paper in 2004.

More local news: [Brackendale and other neighbourhoods](/neighbourhoods/).

stories.head: Woodfibre now plans months of flaring, not weeks. How to comment by Nov 29
stories.dek: When Woodfibre LNG was approved in 2015, start up flaring was expected to last three to four weeks. The company now says commissioning will take six to eight months, with flaring several days a week. Comments on its air emissions permit are open until November 29.
stories.take: Email comments on the air emissions permit to info@wlng.ca, copying waste.management@bc-er.ca, by November 29, or ask questions at one of four open houses.
stories.body:
## Weeks then, months now

When Woodfibre LNG was approved, its [2015 flaring report](https://projects.eao.gov.bc.ca/api/public/document/588691c3e036fb010576901c/download/Planned%20and%20Emergency%20Flaring%20Supplemental%20Report,%20June%202015..pdf) said start up and commissioning would take about three to four weeks, with flaring bursts of up to three or four days at a time. It said flaring would happen less than 3% of the time overall, never during normal operation apart from small pilot lights, and about once a year for planned maintenance.

The company's plan today, as presented at its October open house and in its new air emissions permit application, is different:

- Commissioning now runs about **six to eight months**, with flaring several days a week.
- After the first LNG cargo, about **two years** of stabilizing operations follow, with flaring decreasing.
- About **three years** after commissioning, flaring drops to less than once a month.

Woodfibre's communications director, Sean Beardow, told The Squamish Chief the company is being "very forthright" that commissioning flaring will last longer and happen more often. Tracey Saxby of My Sea to Sky said the project was approved on what she called a false premise.

## What you would see and hear

These are the company's own modelled numbers:

- **Flame:** up to 60 metres above a 134 metre flare stack, or up to 90 metres in a rare emergency.
- **Light:** 5.4 lux at Britannia Beach, 3.4 lux in Squamish and 1.3 lux at Furry Creek during flaring. A typical street light is 10 to 15 lux.
- **Noise:** up to 6 decibels louder at Britannia Beach and 2.5 decibels in Squamish and Stá7mes.
- **Smoke:** during unplanned flaring, black smoke is allowed for up to 15 minutes in any two hour window. Longer counts as non compliance.
- **Air:** Woodfibre says its modelling keeps pollution in nearby communities below B.C.'s Air Quality Objectives, and that communities will be told before flaring happens.

A University of Victoria study published in September 2025 found LNG plants worldwide flare about three times more gas during start up than in normal running, and that start up lasted about two years on average. It named Woodfibre among Canadian projects whose assessments did not model start up flaring ([summary](https://cape.ca/press_release/first-peer-reviewed-global-study-finds-three-times-more-gas-is-flared-during-lng-facilities-start-up-phase-with-proponents-in-b-c-and-canada-not-modelling-these-in-environmental-assessment/)).

In October 2025, after that study came out, Jeremy Valeriote, then the BC Green MLA for West Vancouver Sea to Sky, called on the province to stop LNG expansion, including Woodfibre, and to count flaring in emissions reporting and environmental assessments ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/sea-to-sky-mla-calls-for-halt-to-lng-expansion-over-flaring-health-concerns-11307853)). My Sea to Sky asked the province to require full modelling of start up flaring, including for projects already approved.

## How to comment by November 29

Woodfibre filed the air emissions permit application with the BC Energy Regulator on October 28 ([announcement](https://woodfibrelng.ca/news/2026/10/29/woodfibre-lng-submits-air-emissions-permit-application-to-bc-energy-regulator/)). It covers the flares, a furnace, a thermal oxidizer, backup diesel generators and fire pumps, and plant vents.

- **Who:** anyone who thinks they may be affected by the plant's air emissions.
- **Deadline:** Sunday, November 29.
- **Email:** info@wlng.ca, with a copy to the BC Energy Regulator at waste.management@bc-er.ca. Woodfibre collects the comments and passes them to the regulator.
- **Ideas for what to ask:** a side by side of the 2015 and current flaring plans, full emissions totals for commissioning, independent checks of noise and light, and whether the provincial Environmental Assessment Office has looked at the change.

## Open houses

Woodfibre is holding four drop in open houses on this permit and a second one for stormwater ([details](https://woodfibrelng.ca/news/2026/10/29/youre-invited-upcoming-open-houses-on-waste-discharge-authorization-wda-permit-applications/)):

- **Britannia Beach Community Hall,** 101 Church Street: Tuesday, November 17 and Wednesday, December 2, 4:30 to 7:30 p.m.
- **Executive Suites,** 40900 Tantalus Road, Squamish: Thursday, November 19 and Thursday, December 3, 4:30 to 7:30 p.m.

The Squamish Chief [reported the open house details and flaring figures](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/udpate-public-comment-period-open-for-woodfibre-lng-air-emissions-application-12855424). More background is on our [Woodfibre LNG page](/issues/woodfibre-lng/).

stories.head: Squamish's Jenna Stoner led B.C.'s towns and cities. Why she's been replaced
stories.dek: Jenna Stoner, elected president of the Union of BC Municipalities in September, has been replaced because she no longer sits on Squamish council. Fraser Lake Mayor Sarrah Storey takes over for 2026 to 2027. Stoner's loss to Mayor Sean Easton also ends her roles on the regional district and hospital district boards.
stories.take: Mayor Sean Easton and Councillors Sarah Ellis and Eric Andersen will represent Squamish on the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board, which first meets November 26.
stories.body:
## Why Stoner was replaced

Jenna Stoner was elected president of the Union of BC Municipalities at its yearly convention in September. The group's bylaws say its leaders must hold a seat on a local council. Stoner ran for mayor of Squamish in the October 17 local elections and lost to [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/). Since she no longer sits on council, the union had to replace her.

In a news release, the union thanked Stoner for her years on its board and her commitment to her community. It also thanked all board members who were not re-elected this fall.

The Squamish Chief [reported the change](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/fraser-lake-mayor-succeeds-squamishs-jenna-stoner-as-head-of-ubcm-12986175).

## Who leads the union now

- **Sarrah Storey**, who had been first vice president, is now president for the 2026 to 2027 term. She was re-elected Mayor of Fraser Lake on October 17.
- **Keith Pagel**, a Nelson councillor, moves up to first vice president.

The union is more than 100 years old. It speaks for local governments across B.C. and brings their concerns to the provincial and federal governments as one voice.

## Stoner's time in office

- Eight years as a Squamish councillor
- Four years on the union's executive before becoming president, moving from director at large to third, second and then first vice president

Losing her council seat also means Stoner no longer serves as a Squamish director on the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board, or as chair of the Sea to Sky Hospital District board.

## Who represents Squamish on the regional board

At the new council's [inaugural meeting](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/), members voted on who will sit on the regional district board for this term:

- [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/)
- [Councillor Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/)
- [Councillor Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/)

The regional district board holds its own inaugural meeting on November 26. For more on how local government works, see our [plain guide to council](/how-council-works/).
